project.name: Health Supply Chain Network Design
project.summary: A living map of a country's health supply chain that shows what it costs to reach every clinic — by road, boat and plane, month by month — and who gets left out when money is saved.

features.name: Usable by everyone
features.oneLiner: The whole screen works with a keyboard, reads correctly aloud, and holds up on a small display.

needsYou.title: The latest work is saved and waiting for your go-ahead
needsYou.text: All 23 accessibility checks pass and the 288 automatic tests are green. It is saved on its own copy — nothing has been added to the main project until you say so.

pieces.name: Text you can actually read
Every control reachable without a mouse
Buttons big enough for a finger
Holds together on a narrow screen
Automatic check that catches slips

versions.note: Saved and checked. Waiting for your go-ahead before it joins the main project.

decisions.what: Buttons stay small for a mouse and grow to finger size only on a touch screen, so neither gets a compromise.
The check runs itself and fails loudly, so this cannot quietly rot later.

unsure: There is no light-colour version of the screen — it is dark only.
It stacks and stays usable on a phone, but has had no proper phone-first design pass.

activity.what: All 23 checks passed, on all nine panels, at six screen widths
Six controls that only worked with a mouse now work with a keyboard too
Faint grey text that most of the explanations were written in was too pale to read — darkened it

features.name: The map
features.oneLiner: Every clinic, store and delivery route in the country on one screen you can read at a glance.

pieces.name: Coastline drawn without needing internet
Clinics coloured by how well they are supplied
Delivery routes by road, sea, air and river
Optional online map underneath

versions.note: Shows 134 clinics, 5 stores and 39 timetabled services across Papua New Guinea.

decisions.what: The map must work with no internet at all. A provincial office often has none, so the coastline ships with the tool and online maps are an optional extra on top.
Decided against switching to Mapbox for the map. It needs internet and a paid key, and would not change any answer.

unsure: The coastline we draw is deliberately rough — good to about 4km. Fine for showing where things are, not for measuring.

activity.what: Looked at using Mapbox instead and decided the current approach is better here
Ten real towns were being marked as out at sea — the coastline was wrong and is now fixed

features.name: Comparing plans side by side
features.oneLiner: Run several 'what if' plans at once and see cost, coverage and risk in one table.

pieces.name: Seven ready-made plans to compare
Run them all at the same time
Every plan measured against how things work today
Download the results as a spreadsheet

versions.note: Today's network costs 11.24M kina a year and reaches everyone. Cutting cost saves 19.5%.

decisions.what: Instead of forcing every plan to reach everyone, we put a price on not reaching someone. Every plan now gives an answer you can read, rather than some simply failing.

unsure: The costs, demand and boat timetables in the demo are illustrative, not the ministry's real figures. The clinic locations and the shape of the network are real.

activity.what: Running seven plans at once was occasionally failing — found the cause and fixed it
Opening three new stores looked like it cost 4.5M a year more than it does — the one-off building cost was being counted as a yearly bill

features.name: Who pays for a saving
features.oneLiner: Shows which communities lose their supply when a plan saves money — before anyone decides.

pieces.name: Sorts every clinic into five groups by how hard it is to reach
Names the people affected, not just a percentage
Lets you set a floor nobody can fall below

versions.note: Cutting cost by 19.5% moves 217,480 people from supplied to not supplied. Setting a floor holds them at 90% and still saves 9.3%.

decisions.what: Fairness is part of the sum, not a report at the end. A plan that saves money by giving up on the hardest-to-reach fifth has to say so in the same breath.

unsure: How we decide which communities are hardest to reach is our own definition. A ministry may well use a different one, and can change it.

activity.what: Checked the numbers hold up both ways round — the saving and the abandonment are the same figure seen from two sides

features.name: Month by month conditions
features.oneLiner: See what the wet season does — which roads close, and who can only be reached by plane.

pieces.name: Twelve months of road, sea and air access
Shows which routes shut, and when
Re-prices the whole plan for that month

versions.note: In February 19 clinics cannot be reached at all and the plan costs 35.8% more than a normal month.

decisions.what: Every route carries twelve monthly access figures from the start, so the seasons are built in rather than bolted on later.

unsure: The seasonal patterns come from typical weather, not from records of roads actually closing. Worth checking with provincial staff before publishing anything.

activity.what: February and July had no workable answer at all — changed the approach so every month gives a readable result naming who is affected

features.name: Getting your own data in
features.oneLiner: Download a spreadsheet, fill it in, upload it back. It is checked before anything is saved.

pieces.name: Blank template to fill in
37 checks on what you upload
See every problem before anything is saved
Export everything back out again

versions.note: Four sheets, 70 columns. The file you download and the file you upload are the same shape.

decisions.what: Nothing is saved until you have seen the check results and said go ahead. A half-finished import is worse than one that stops, because nobody can tell which half is real.
What you download and what you upload have identical columns, so the work survives even if this tool does not.

unsure: Starting a brand new country still means filling in a blank spreadsheet of 70 columns. That is a lot of work somewhere with little existing data.
Only Excel files are accepted. No CSV, and no older .xls.

activity.what: Checked that exporting everything and importing it straight back changes nothing

features.name: Connecting to a country's own systems
features.oneLiner: Pull the clinic list and consumption straight out of the systems a ministry already runs.

pieces.name: DHIS2
OpenLMIS
Open mSupply
Matches incoming clinics to ones already on file
Preview every change before saving
Tried against a real ministry system

versions.note: Works end to end against a stand-in server: 6 clinics matched, 1 new, 1 moved, 1 renamed.

decisions.what: A sync never touches the delivery routes. No stock system knows about boats, and losing the timetables would destroy the hardest part of the model to rebuild.
Passwords can stay outside the tool entirely, so they never end up in a backup of it.

unsure: Tested against a stand-in server we built ourselves, not a real ministry system. It needs one real connection before anyone relies on it.
Papua New Guinea's own mSupply is an older version that does not offer this kind of connection. The spreadsheet route is the one that works there today.
A sync has to be started by hand. It does not run on a schedule.

activity.what: A full pull, preview and save worked over a real network connection
Two different clinics in the same town were being treated as one place because their names were trimmed too aggressively — fixed

features.name: The costed plan of action
features.oneLiner: Turns a chosen scenario into a phased list of what to do, what it costs, and in what order.

pieces.name: Phases in the order they have to happen
A cost against each step
Exports with the rest of the results

versions.note: Every scenario can be turned into a phased plan with the full one-off costs shown separately from the yearly ones.

decisions.what: One-off building costs are shown separately from yearly running costs, so a plan cannot look cheaper than it is.

unsure: How long each phase takes is an estimate, not drawn from how long this work actually takes in practice.

activity.what: Checked the roadmap costs add up to the same total the scenario reports

features.name: Selling this beyond one country
features.oneLiner: Turning a Papua New Guinea tool into something a consultant anywhere can pay to use.

pieces.name: Work out what has to be built
Work out who would pay and how much
Decide how the money works
Set up a second country
Accounts and logins
Taking payment

decisions.what: Looked at what already works across countries and what does not. The way the information is stored already handles many countries; what is entirely missing is accounts, logins and payment.

unsure: How the money works is unresolved. The promise is that the tool stays with the government after the consultant leaves — but if the consultant is the one paying, who pays next year?
The consultants this would be sold to lost most of their funding in 2025. The need went up; the number of people with a budget went down.
The estimate of a few hundred people who would pay is our own guess, not a figure from anywhere.

activity.what: Wrote up what to build and what the market looks like, with the honest version of both

parkingLot.name: Better-looking offline map
parkingLot.note: A sharper map that still needs no internet. The genuinely useful version of the Mapbox idea we turned down.

parkingLot.name: Real road distances
parkingLot.note: The tool already has a place for this to plug into. Until it does, road distances are informed estimates and say so.

parkingLot.name: Collecting data on phones in the field
parkingLot.note: For countries where the information does not exist yet and has to be gathered. Nothing started.

parkingLot.name: Accounts, logins and payment
parkingLot.note: Needed before anyone could pay for access. Nothing exists yet — planned out, not begun.

parkingLot.name: Mapbox as the map
parkingLot.note: Looked at properly and set aside: it needs internet and a paid key, and would not change any answer the tool gives. The reasoning is written down.
